analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to show patients their out-of-pocket costs before care and publish what they pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in July 2023, it sat in House committees and a subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code, the Public Health Service Act, and the employer-benefit law (ERISA) to require group health plans and insurers to tell individuals, on request, what they would pay out of pocket for a specific service — including how far along they are on their deductible and whether prior approval rules apply [S2]. It would also require plans and insurers to publish their negotiated in-network rates and what they actually paid, including for drugs net of rebates, in machine-readable public files every few months, with plain-language instructions and help for people with limited English or disabilities [S2]. Nothing in it would change prices directly; it would force disclosure so people can shop and compare [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: People covered by employer or other private health plans gain the right to a real-time estimate of what a specific service will cost them — their deductible status, copay, whether prior authorization applies — through a website tool or by phone or paper at no charge [S2]. Researchers, employers, and consumer tools also gain access to quarterly machine-readable files showing negotiated rates, out-of-network payments, and drug prices net of rebates, so they can compare plans and spot wide price differences for the same care [S2]. Plans must post instructions in plain language and provide translations and assistive services for people with limited English proficiency or disabilities [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Gives every enrollee a no-cost, real-time estimate of their cost sharing for a specific item or service — in-network rate, deductible progress, copay or coinsurance, and any prior authorization or step-therapy requirement — through a website tool or, at their choice, by paper, phone, or other electronic means

Requires plans to publish their negotiated in-network rates, out-of-network billed and paid amounts, and drug payments net of rebates in machine-readable public files, updated quarterly (monthly for drug data), free and without a login, in a format that lets people compare across plans

Makes plans attest that published price information is complete and accurate, and requires plain-language instructions plus translations and assistive services for people with limited English proficiency and disabilities

Uses a bipartisan pairing — Republican sponsor Brian Fitzpatrick with Democrat Susie Lee of Nevada as an original cosponsor — and covers employer plans, individual coverage, and self-insured plans through parallel amendments to the tax code, the Public Health Service Act, and ERISA

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group plans bear the cost of building the real-time cost-sharing tool, publishing and maintaining quarterly machine-readable rate files, and providing translations and assistive services [S2]. Insurers and hospital systems also lose the confidentiality of negotiated rates and net-of-rebate drug payments, which can weaken their bargaining positions; some of the compliance cost could show up in premiums [S2].

drawbacks.text: Insurers and employers would shoulder significant compliance costs — real-time tools, quarterly data publication in a usable standard format, attestations, and translation and assistive services — and some of that cost could be passed to customers through premiums

Publishing in-network rates and net-of-rebate drug payments exposes negotiated discounts; providers and hospitals can see what competitors charge, which in some cases lets them demand higher rates, so transparency does not guarantee prices fall

Much of the disclosure already exists by regulation under the 2020 Transparency in Coverage rule, and the bill expressly leaves that rule in place for earlier plan years — so the practical gain over the status quo is codifying the rules into law and adding features like prior-authorization disclosure and plain-language instructions, not an entirely new right

Raw machine-readable files listing rates for every provider and billing code are difficult for ordinary consumers to use directly; the bill relies on third parties to turn the data into usable comparisons

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: patients get to see costs before care and researchers get the underlying data, which over time can pressure prices down and expose extreme variation. The costs are compliance burdens on insurers and employers and the risk that publishing negotiated rates sometimes helps providers raise them. On balance a consumer-favorable, low-drama bill — but because a 2020 regulation already requires much of this disclosure, the bill's practical impact is an upgrade and legal permanence rather than a first-of-its-kind right.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees in July 2023 and then to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it sat without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) introduced the bill on July 26, 2023, joined as original cosponsor by Susie Lee (D-NV), and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees.
Two days later, on July 28, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, a step short of a full committee vote.
The bill drew a total of 2 cosponsors, both Democrats, and no further action for over a year.

On December 17, 2024, with weeks left before the Congress ended, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health again; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors avoided new statutory disclosure duties and the compliance costs of building real-time cost-sharing tools and publishing negotiated rates; hospitals and provider groups kept the confidentiality of their negotiated prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and providers kept price confidentiality

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to build real-time cost-sharing tools and publish negotiated in-network rates, out-of-network payments, and net-of-rebate drug prices publicly. That exposure weakens their ability to keep negotiated discounts secret and adds compliance costs that could flow into premiums.

Quarterly publication of what each plan pays each provider makes their negotiated prices comparable across the market, letting patients and employers spot providers charging far more for the same service and giving them leverage to push rates down.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug pricing intermediaries
industries.note: The bill requires plans to disclose what they actually paid for each drug net of rebates, discounts, and price concessions — the figure PBMs and insurers usually keep confidential — which would expose the spread between list price and net cost.
Employers would face compliance costs for plans they sponsor, but they also gain access to published rate data that helps them judge whether insurers' network prices are competitive.
Mandated machine-readable files and standardized formats create raw material for consumer comparison websites and analytics firms to build tools on top of.
